value.overview: The Gray Catbird (Dumetella carolinensis) is a medium-sized songbird of the mockingbird family, recognized by its slate-gray body, black cap, dark wings and tail, and chestnut undertail coverts. It often stays concealed in dense vegetation but gives distinctive mewing calls and varied, musical phrases. The species breeds widely across eastern and central North America and migrates south in winter, reaching Mexico, Central America, and parts of the Caribbean.
value.classification: The Gray Catbird belongs to the family Mimidae, which includes mockingbirds and thrashers. It is the only species in the genus Dumetella.
value.identification: Adults are about 20–24 cm long and have uniform slate-gray plumage, a blackish cap, black wings and tail, and conspicuous rusty-red undertail coverts that may be difficult to see when the bird is perched. The bill and eyes are dark. Its long tail is often cocked or flicked. The species is usually detected by its catlike mewing call, although it also produces a complex series of whistles, chatters, and imitations.
value.rangeHabitat: The Gray Catbird breeds from the central and eastern United States north into southern Canada, with some breeding populations farther west. In winter it occurs from the southern United States and Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a regular migrant and winter visitor, most frequent in Caribbean-slope lowlands, especially below about 500 m, though individuals can occur as high as 1,500 m. It uses dense second growth, hedgerows, forest edges, gardens, and other shrubby habitats.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory in Costa Rica. It usually arrives on the Caribbean slope from September or early October, becomes most noticeable in October and November, and may remain until late April or early May. Spring passage is less conspicuous and is concentrated along the Caribbean coast. It is occasional in the Central Valley and on the southern Pacific slope.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly in dense shrubs, woodland edges, regenerating forest, hedgerows, swamps, and suburban vegetation across North America. The female generally builds a bulky, open cup nest of twigs, grasses, bark, and other plant material in thick cover, often close to the ground. A clutch commonly contains three to five bluish-green eggs. Both adults feed the nestlings, and pairs may raise more than one brood in a season.
value.dietFeeding: The Gray Catbird eats insects and other invertebrates, including beetles, ants, caterpillars, grasshoppers, and spiders. Fruits and berries become especially important during migration and winter. It usually forages in dense shrubs and low vegetation, picking insects from leaves or the ground and taking fruit from bushes. Its flexible diet allows it to use forest edges, gardens, hedgerows, and other habitats with abundant cover and seasonal food.
value.behavior: This species is active but often secretive, moving through thick vegetation with deliberate hops and short flights. It commonly flicks or raises its long tail and may forage alone or in loose groups, especially during migration. Gray Catbirds are accomplished singers that combine whistles, harsh notes, mewing sounds, and imitations into extended songs. They defend breeding territories, but wintering birds in Costa Rica are generally scattered and less territorial.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to face a major immediate conservation risk, although regional monitoring has documented declines in some areas.
